title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10=4, n01=0) yields p = 0.125 via p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n=4, p=0.5). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered confirmatory decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative task diagnostics, and point readers to the archived execution manifest for the human‑readable verifier codebook and all artifact hashes.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort, but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Modern large language models (LLMs) show promise for intent translation but exhibit hallucination and factual errors that threaten operational safety. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate change with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow/policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We contribute: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) a detailed, artifact‑grounded description of the generation protocol, verifier semantics, and repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (exact conditional McNemar) and exploratory bootstrap descriptions with explicit handling of small‑discordant‑count behavior; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and an explicit discussion of verifier blind spots and external validity constraints.
sections.related_work: Three converging literatures motivate this study. Surveys and system papers document interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps tasks (intent translation, AIOps, multi‑agent orchestration) while emphasizing hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers. Tool‑augmented and agentic LLM architectures that call external verifiers, simulators, or validators have been proposed to improve reliability; deterministic verifiers derived from configuration analysis tools (Batfish and related systems) can check ordering, availability/group constraints, and final‑state properties prior to deployment. Prior empirical evaluations of tool‑augmented designs vary in scale and seldom present preregistered paired trials that execute identical generator outputs under guarded and unguarded conditions with a deterministic adjudicator. These gaps motivated our controlled paired design and the choice to use a deterministic verifier as the operational adjudicator. Representative prior works that informed verifier design and evaluation framing are cited and verified in the evidence bundle.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) over N=500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles (synthetic_topologies_v1). Sampling seeds and the deterministic task generator were frozen in the preregistration. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as an exploratory descriptor. The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08; realized margins differed (see Results).
Generation and orchestration semantics: Each intent produced a single shared_initial_generation candidate using the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; model_config SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification failed the pipeline invoked at most one automated repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 504 and completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions). The execution manifest and raw result file are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02; execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256: 5a822e787302a0b3bb03a86a81b20564a44e2636731f853f9d45ac12e4876cc8).
Deterministic verifier adjudication semantics (artifact grounded): deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs a fixed sequence of checks on a normalized CLI sequence: (i) syntactic parsing and normalization to a canonical command form, (ii) workflow/required‑sequence checks (must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change patterns), (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active / minimum_active_in_groups), (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes), and (v) final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the validator emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and valid=true/false. Representative validator_trace objects are archived under execution/scoring/ (see Disclosure). The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) and its SHA‑256 are enumerated in the archived execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) inside the evidence bundle; consult that manifest for the explicit codebook artifact path and its hash.
Statistical procedures: Primary confirmatory inference used the conditional exact McNemar test on the discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01). For reproducibility we report the applied computation: the two‑sided conditional p‑value = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ k; n, 0.5), where k is the number of discordants favoring GVR (n10). Per preregistration we also report the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed by resampling the paired outcomes with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration treated the bootstrap CI as descriptive/exploratory when discordant counts are small. Missingness handling: primary analysis uses complete pairs; pre‑registered sensitivity treats technical failures as unsafe. In this run, there were zero failed episodes.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary counts: completed_episode_count = 1000; model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. These archived counts are the direct inputs to the preregistered confirmatory test and appear in analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256: 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece).
Confirmatory test (preregistered): observed discordants n = 4 with k = n10 = 4 (all discordants favor GVR). Applying the exact conditional McNemar formula yields p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test is the preregistered decision rule, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.
Exploratory paired bootstrap CI: the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. As pre‑specified, this CI is descriptive: with near‑ceiling margins and only four discordants the bootstrap percentile CI can exclude zero while the exact conditional McNemar is non‑significant. The preregistration labeled the bootstrap as exploratory in this small‑discordant regime.
Repair invocation and cost diagnostics: repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; all four repaired candidates were accepted after repair (the four n10 pairs). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008. Provider‑call accounting in deterministic_reconciliation.json records stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4; hosted_model_call_event_count = 504; cache_hit_count = 0. These reconciliation artifacts are archived (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256: 48bafa8c94272b409a7329e4946995f633a5de7789e5a96fdcef72d3bb127ffe).
Representative example (artifact‑grounded): pair-000001 (task-000001) shows a medium‑difficulty shutdown_configure_restore pattern. The shared_initial candidate (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) matches the reference answer; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, observed_touched_field_count = 3, and valid = true in both pre/post validation traces for this task (detailed JSON scoring artifact: execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json; representative SHA‑256s are listed in the Disclosure). Table 2 lists six anonymized representative tasks (task-000001..task-000006) with their difficulty labels and required_sequence summaries drawn directly from task_manifest entries.
Secondary arms and preregistered but unexecuted comparisons: the preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed in this archived run; the multiplicity plan therefore could not be fully applied. The absence of that arm is reported in the execution manifest and Disclosure.
sections.discussion:
Synthesis under preregistered inferential rules: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; these correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Under the preregistered exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125) we do not claim confirmatory significance. The exploratory bootstrap CI indicates a small positive effect but must be interpreted cautiously given the very small discordant count and near‑ceiling margins.
Why tests diverge: the conditional exact McNemar conditions on fixed margins and evaluates the binomial tail of discordant outcomes; with n=4 and k=4 this yields p=0.125. The paired bootstrap resamples paired outcomes without conditioning on margins and can produce a percentile CI excluding zero even when conditional McNemar is non‑significant. This reflects differing inferential targets and small‑sample instability rather than contradictory evidence. We therefore follow the preregistered decision rule and label the bootstrap CI as exploratory.
Verifier fidelity and blind spots: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces syntactic normalization, workflow/required‑sequence checks, group/availability constraints, dependency and paired‑field enforcement, and final‑state equality to expected_final_state. It does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane convergence timing, hardware‑level side effects, or emergent cross‑component interaction beyond the encoded rules. Passing the verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) and its artifact entry are enumerated in the archived execution manifest (see Disclosure); reviewers and auditors can examine the manifest to recover the explicit codebook artifact path and its SHA‑256.
Threats to validity: internal validity is strong (preregistered paired design, fixed seeds, complete pairs). Construct validity is limited by verifier abstraction: the chosen validation rules represent an operational subset (ordering, availability, paired fields), but omit vendor timing and some control‑plane convergence hazards. External validity is constrained by synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1 (vendor‑agnostic CLI templates), and single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini). Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan assumed larger baseline discordance (~0.08 effect target); the observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs and reduced realized inferential sensitivity.
Operational implications: GVR with a compact verifier can intercept verifier‑detectable hazards at low LLM overhead in synthetic workloads. The practical value depends critically on verifier coverage: broad verifier coverage of production hazards (vendor semantics, convergence effects) is required before GVR can be claimed ready for production automation. Cost/latency trade‑offs (invoking heavyweight verifiers) were not measured here and remain an operational next step.
Reproducibility and artifact access: all primary execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle. Key artifact SHA‑256 values cited in the Disclosure enable independent verification of the reported counts (example: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 fe9b93ef..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2..., analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 8fb135ce..., analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 f3e19742..., analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 48bafa8c...). The full execution_manifest.json inside the bundle enumerates every artifact path and its SHA‑256, including the human‑readable verifier codebook artifact (consult execution/execution_manifest.json for the explicit codebook path and hash).
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N=500) using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator. All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived for independent verification.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
